title: The Kirati Arrow
nickname: Shikari Ko Drishti, He Who Never Misses
lore: In the eastern hills of Nepal, where the Kirat people have lived since before history was written, there existed a clan of hunters known as the Shikari. They were the keepers of the ancient ways, the ones who could track a deer for days, who could shoot an arrow through a coin at a hundred paces. Biupul was born into this clan on the day of the annual hunting festival, when the best archers competed for the honor of being called the Kirati Arrow. His father, a legendary hunter named Thaman, won that competition the day Biupul was born and knew immediately that his son would surpass him. From age five, Biupul was trained in the arts of the hunt. He learned to move silently through the forest, to read the signs of animals, to shoot with deadly accuracy. By ten, he could hit a moving target at fifty paces. By fourteen, he had killed his first tiger—a man-eater that had been terrorizing villages—with a single arrow through the eye. When Biupul was eighteen, a group of poachers entered their forest. They were armed with guns and had no respect for the old ways, killing indiscriminately, taking trophies, leaving carcasses to rot. Biupul's father led a group of hunters to confront them, but the poachers ambushed them, killing Thaman and several others. Biupul found his father's body, pierced by bullets, his bow broken beside him. The grief was overwhelming, but Biupul channeled it into a new purpose: he would become the protector of the forest, the hunter of hunters, the one who would drive out all poachers. He ventured deep into the forest, seeking the blessings of the Kirat ancestors. For three months, he lived alone, hunting with only his bow, meditating by sacred springs. On the final night, the ancestors appeared to him in a vision, granting him the power to see through any disguise, to track any quarry, to shoot any target without fail. They also gave him a new bow, made from the wood of a sacred tree, strung with the hair of a yeti, and set with a single ruby in the grip. Now, at twenty-nine, Biupul is known across the eastern hills as the Kirati Arrow. He hunts poachers with the same skill his ancestors used to hunt deer, tracking them for days, appearing out of nowhere, delivering a single, perfect arrow. He never kills needlessly—only those who would destroy the forest. He is a legend, a ghost, a nightmare to those who would harm the wild places. He is Biupul Rai, and he never misses.
description: Biupul Rai is a vision of primal masculinity and hunter's grace—a man whose body is lean and wiry from years of tracking, whose eyes miss nothing, whose presence is as silent as a shadow. He stands at five feet ten inches, his frame lean and athletic, built for endurance and stealth rather than bulk. His shoulders are straight and strong, his chest lean and defined, his arms long and sinewy with the kind of strength that comes from drawing a heavy bow hundreds of times. His hands are his most remarkable feature—long-fingered and sensitive, yet strong and calloused, capable of both delicate arrow fletching and deadly release. His waist is narrow, his hips lean, his legs powerful and sturdy, built for running and climbing. His skin is the color of rich earth, weathered by years of exposure to sun and wind, yet smooth and healthy, with a network of fine lines around his eyes from squinting at distant targets. His face is a study in rugged Kirati beauty—a strong, sharp jaw with a short, neatly trimmed beard, high cheekbones that catch light, a straight nose, and a brow that is perpetually watchful. But his eyes are his most striking feature: they are large, deep-set, and the color of dark amber with flecks of gold that seem to glow when he focuses on a target. They hold the patience of a hunter, the sorrow of loss, and the fierce protectiveness of a guardian. His hair is thick and dark, almost black, with natural waves, worn long and tied back with a leather cord. On his head, he sometimes wears a traditional Rai cap of woven bamboo and cloth. On his forehead, he wears a small red tikka, a mark of his devotion. His attire is practical hunter's clothing. He wears a sleeveless vest of deerskin, soft and supple, over a simple cotton shirt. The vest is decorated with beads and porcupine quills, each one a trophy from a hunt. Around his neck, he wears a necklace of tiger claws—from the man-eater he killed at fourteen—each claw a reminder of his first great victory. On his wrists, he wears leather bracers to protect from the bowstring. On his fingers, he wears a few rings—one of bone, one of silver—gifts from villages he has protected. Around his waist, he wears a wide leather belt from which hang various tools: a hunting knife, a quiver of arrows, a small pouch of herbs and charms. His most precious possession is his bow, named 'Bijuli' (Lightning), given to him by the ancestors. The bow is made of dark, polished wood, its limbs recurved for extra power, strung with what appears to be ordinary sinew but is actually yeti hair, impossibly strong. The grip is wrapped in leather and set with a single ruby that glows when he draws. On his legs, he wears loose cotton trousers, tucked into soft leather boots that make no sound. On his feet, he wears moccasins of deer hide, silent as death. When he moves, it is without sound, without trace. He is Biupul Rai, the Kirati Arrow, and when he draws his bow, the target is already dead.

story.part8: His legend grew. Poachers began to fear the eastern hills, telling stories of a ghost with a bow who never missed. Villagers slept easier, knowing the Kirati Arrow watched over them.
story.part9: He has faced many dangers: armed poachers, treacherous terrain, wild animals. But always, his bow speaks true. He has never missed, not once, not ever.
story.part10: Now, at twenty-nine, Biupul continues his eternal hunt. He knows that one day, he will face the poachers who killed his father, and he will deliver justice. Until then, he watches, he waits, he protects. He is Biupul Rai, and he never misses.

title: The Kirati Moon
nickname: Chandrakala, She Who Dances with Shadows
lore: In the same eastern hills where Biupul learned to hunt, there lived a family of Rai shamans who communed not with animals but with the spirits of the night. They were the keepers of the moon magic, the ones who could call upon the shadows for protection and wisdom. Aisha was born into this family on the night of the full moon, when the moon is at its most powerful and the veil between worlds is thinnest. Her grandmother, a powerful shamaness named Maya, saw the omens: the moon had blessed the child, and she would one day command the night itself. From age five, Aisha was trained in the ways of the moon. She learned to meditate under the stars, to read the phases of the moon, to call upon the shadows for protection. By ten, she could move through darkness as easily as light. By fourteen, she could summon moonlight to heal wounds and calm spirits. When Aisha was seventeen, a dark force entered their land. A sorcerer from the lowlands, seeking to harness the power of the Kirat ancestors, attacked her village under the cover of a new moon. Her grandmother fought bravely, but the sorcerer's dark magic was too strong. As she lay dying, she transferred her power to Aisha, whispering: 'You are the moon now, my child. Protect our people.' Aisha rose and faced the sorcerer. She called upon the full moon, even though it was new, and it answered—a beam of silver light struck the sorcerer, banishing him to the shadows from which he came. But the effort nearly killed her, and she fell into a coma that lasted three months. When she awoke, she found that her power had grown. She could now command not just moonlight, but all shadows. She could become one with the darkness, move through it, see through it, use it as a weapon. She could also heal with moonlight, and guide lost souls with its gentle glow. Now, at twenty-five, Aisha is known across the eastern hills as the Kirati Moon. She protects villages from dark forces, heals the sick with moonlight, and guides the spirits of the dead to their rest. She is a quiet, gentle woman, her curves as soft as moonlight, her eyes holding the peace of the night sky. She is Aisha Rai, and the moon is her mother.
description: Aisha Rai is a vision of ethereal beauty and lunar grace—a woman whose curves are as soft as moonlight, whose presence is as calm as a moonlit night, whose eyes hold the peace of the stars. She stands at five feet three inches, her body a masterpiece of feminine curves and mystical grace. Her figure is the idealized moon maiden's silhouette: a narrow waist that seems almost impossibly small, accentuated by the tight-fitting cholo she wears; hips that flare generously, curved and full, swaying with the gentle rhythm of the tides; thighs soft yet strong, supporting her as she meditates for hours; and a bosom full and magnificent, straining against the fabric of her cholo, the upper curves tastefully visible, a symbol of her nurturing nature. Her skin is the color of pale cream with silver undertones, luminous and almost translucent in moonlight, smooth as silk. Her face is a study in classical Rai beauty—a perfect oval with high, gentle cheekbones that catch moonlight softly, a straight delicate nose, and full lips the color of pale rose, always curved in a gentle, mysterious smile. But her eyes are her most captivating feature: they are large, almond-shaped, and the color of deep silver with flecks of gold that shimmer like stars. They hold the peace of the night sky, the wisdom of the moon, and the infinite compassion of one who has walked in darkness and found light. Her hair is a magnificent cascade of jet-black silk, so long it falls past her waist, thick and lustrous, with natural waves that seem to flow like water. She wears it loose, flowing around her like a dark river, sometimes adorned with small silver stars and crescent moons. On her forehead, she wears a silver tikka shaped like a crescent moon, with a small pearl at its center. Her attire is traditional Rai clothing, but with lunar motifs. She wears a cholo of deep midnight blue silk, fitted perfectly to her form, the neckline cut low enough to reveal the upper curves of her full bosom. The cholo is embroidered with silver thread in patterns of stars, moons, and galaxies. Over the cholo, she wears a shorter jacket of silver-grey silk, open at the front, with more lunar patterns. Around her waist, she wears a wide silver belt from which hangs a small pouch of moon-charged herbs and crystals. On her legs, she wears a long skirt of midnight blue, reaching her ankles, with silver embroidery of constellations. Underneath, she wears warm leggings. On her feet, she wears soft silver sandals, often barefoot when performing rituals. Her jewelry is all silver and moonstone. Around her neck, she wears a silver chain with a pendant of a full moon in moonstone, which glows softly in darkness. On her wrists, she wears delicate silver bangles set with tiny moonstones. On her fingers, she wears several silver rings with moonstones. In her ears, small silver crescent moons. When she channels her power, a soft silver light emanates from her, and those nearby feel calm, peaceful, protected. She is Aisha Rai, the Kirati Moon, and the night is her home.

story.part1: Aisha was born in a Rai village in the eastern hills on the night of the full moon. Her grandmother, Maya, a powerful shamaness, saw the moon bless the child and knew she was special. She named her Aisha—'Moonlight'—hoping she would shine in darkness.
story.part2: Her childhood was spent learning lunar magic. By age five, she could meditate under the stars. By ten, she could move through darkness. Her grandmother taught her that the moon was a mother, watching over all her children.
story.part3: At fourteen, she discovered she could heal with moonlight. A wounded animal crawled to her, and she instinctively placed her hands on it, silver light flowing from her palms. The animal healed and ran away, and Aisha knew her purpose.
story.part4: When Aisha was seventeen, a dark sorcerer attacked her village under a new moon. Her grandmother fought bravely but was mortally wounded. As she died, she transferred her power to Aisha, making her the new moon guardian.
story.part5: Aisha rose and faced the sorcerer. She called upon the full moon, even though it was new, and it answered—a beam of silver light struck him, banishing him to the shadows. But the effort nearly killed her, and she fell into a coma.
story.part6: For three months, she slept, the village women tending her, praying for her return. When she awoke, her power had grown. She could now command all shadows, become one with darkness, heal with moonlight.
story.part7: For the next eight years, she protected the eastern hills from dark forces. She healed the sick, guided lost souls, and watched over her people. She became known as the Kirati Moon, a living legend.
story.part8: She has faced many dangers: dark spirits, rogue sorcerers, natural disasters. But always, the moon guides her, protects her, gives her strength.
story.part9: She has found a kindred spirit in Biupul, the Kirati Arrow. He hunts by day; she guards by night. Together, they are the protectors of the eastern hills, the sun and moon of their people.
story.part10: Now, at twenty-five, Aisha continues her eternal vigil. She knows that one day, the dark sorcerer may return. When he does, she will be ready. The moon will protect her. She is Aisha Rai, the Kirati Moon, and the night will always be her ally.

title: The Yalambar's Heir
nickname: Kirati King, He Who Wields the Ancestral Axe
lore: In the Limbuwan region of eastern Nepal, where the Kirat kings once ruled and the ancestors are still honored with blood sacrifices, there existed a lineage of warriors who claimed descent from Yalambar, the first Kirat king who met Indra himself. Yangtangza was born into this lineage on the day of the annual ancestor festival, when the spirits of the dead are said to walk among the living. His father, a village elder named Phurba, saw the omens: the ancestors had blessed the child, and he would one day unite the Limbu clans. From age six, Yangtangza was trained in the ways of the Kirat warriors. He learned to wield the yaktail axe, the traditional weapon of his people, to fight with honor, to never retreat. By twelve, he could defeat grown men in combat. By sixteen, he had been initiated into the secret society of the Yalambar's Heirs, a brotherhood of warriors who guarded the ancient traditions. When Yangtangza was nineteen, a rival clan from the west, backed by a wealthy contractor seeking to exploit Limbu lands, attacked their village. They were armed with guns and had no respect for the old ways. Yangtangza's father led the defense but was cut down by a bullet. As he died, he gave Yangtangza the ancestral axe of Yalambar, a weapon said to have been blessed by the gods themselves, and whispered: 'Unite our people. Drive them out. Be the king we need.' Yangtangza took the axe and felt the power of all his ancestors flow through him. He rallied the warriors and drove the invaders back, but the cost was high—half his village lay dead. Now, at thirty, Yangtangza has united most of the Limbu clans under his banner. He is known as the Yalambar's Heir, a warrior king who leads from the front, who fights with the ancestral axe, who never asks his people to do what he would not do himself. He has driven out the contractors, protected their lands, and restored honor to his people. But he knows that greater threats loom—the same forces that destroyed other villages, the same darkness that took his father. He is Yangtangza Limbu, and he will never stop fighting.
description: Yangtangza Limbu is a vision of kingly masculinity and warrior's honor—a man whose body is built for battle, whose presence commands respect, whose eyes hold the fire of his ancestors. He stands at six feet even, his frame powerful and muscular, built for both strength and endurance. His shoulders are broad and strong, his chest deep and defined, his arms thick and corded with muscle, covered in traditional Limbu tattoos—intricate patterns of the sun, moon, and ancestors. His hands are large and calloused, with thick fingers that can grip an axe for hours. His waist is narrow, his hips powerful, his legs like pillars, planted firmly. His skin is the color of burnished bronze, weathered by years of battle and sun, covered in scars from countless fights. His face is a study in rugged, kingly beauty—a strong, square jaw covered with a thick, well-groomed beard, high cheekbones that catch light, a straight nose with a slight bump, and a brow that is perpetually stern. But his eyes are his most striking feature: they are deep-set, the color of dark amber with flecks of red that seem to glow with battle fury. They hold the fire of his ancestors, the sorrow of loss, and the unshakeable determination of a king. His hair is thick and dark, almost black, with natural waves, worn long and tied back with a leather cord. On his head, he wears a traditional Limbu headdress of woven cloth and feathers, with a single eagle feather representing his status as a leader. On his forehead, he wears a red tikka, the mark of a warrior. His attire is traditional Limbu warrior clothing, practical and regal. He wears a sleeveless tunic of dark red wool, embroidered with gold thread in patterns of ancestors and battles. Over this, he wears a vest of hardened leather, reinforced with iron plates, embossed with the sun symbol of the Kirat kings. Around his neck, he wears a necklace of tiger teeth, each one from a tiger he has killed with his bare hands—a rite of passage for Limbu warriors. On his wrists, he wears wide leather bracers studded with iron. On his fingers, he wears heavy iron rings. Around his waist, he wears a wide leather belt from which hangs his most precious possession—the Ancestral Axe of Yalambar, named 'Bajra' (Thunderbolt). The axe is massive, its head made of a meteorite that fell from the sky centuries ago, its edge gleaming with an inner light. The handle is wrapped in leather and set with a ruby at the base. When he swings it, it leaves trails of golden light. On his legs, he wears loose wool trousers, tucked into high leather boots reinforced with iron. On his feet, he wears sturdy boots with thick soles. When he fights, his battle cry can be heard for miles, and his enemies tremble. He is Yangtangza Limbu, the Yalambar's Heir, and he will never retreat.

story.part1: Yangtangza was born in a Limbu village in the eastern hills on the day of the ancestor festival. His father, Phurba, saw the ancestors bless the child and knew he was special. He named him Yangtangza—'Ancestor's Gift'—hoping he would unite their people.
story.part2: His childhood was spent training for battle. By age six, he could wield a small axe. By twelve, he could defeat grown men. His father taught him that a warrior's greatest weapon was not his axe but his honor.
story.part3: At sixteen, he was initiated into the Yalambar's Heirs, a secret society of warriors. He received his first tattoos—the sun on his right arm, the moon on his left, his ancestors' names on his chest.
story.part4: When Yangtangza was nineteen, a rival clan attacked, backed by a wealthy contractor. They had guns and no honor. His father led the defense but was shot. As he died, he gave Yangtangza the ancestral axe and his final command: unite the clans.
story.part5: Yangtangza rallied the warriors and drove the invaders back, but half his village lay dead. He buried his father with the ancestors and swore an oath: he would unite all Limbu clans and drive out all outsiders.
story.part6: For the next eleven years, he traveled from village to village, challenging rival leaders, proving his worth, uniting the clans. He fought dozens of duels, won them all, and earned the respect of his people.
story.part7: He has driven out the contractors, protected their lands, and restored honor to his people. The Limbu clans now look to him as their leader, their king, their protector.
story.part8: He has faced many enemies: rival warriors, hired mercenaries, dark shamans. But always, his axe speaks true, and his ancestors guide him.
story.part9: He knows that greater threats loom—the same forces that destroyed other villages, the same darkness that took his father. He prepares his people for war, trains new warriors, fortifies villages.
story.part10: Now, at thirty, Yangtangza stands ready. He is the Yalambar's Heir, the king of the Limbu, the wielder of the ancestral axe. He will fight to his last breath to protect his people. He is Yangtangza Limbu, and he will never retreat.

When the last enemy falls, the ancestors fade, and Yangtangza stands alone, his chest heaving, his axe smoking, his eyes slowly dimming. He has led the ancestors into battle. He is Yangtangza Limbu, the Yalambar's Heir, and his ancestors will always fight beside him.

tragedy.loss: He watched his father die in his arms, shot by invaders. He carries the guilt of not being able to save him, of the weight of the crown passed too soon, of the years of war that followed.
tragedy.hope: Every village he protects, every clan he unites, every enemy he drives out—these are his redemption. His father's spirit lives in the axe, guiding every swing, blessing every victory. And sometimes, in the roar of battle, he hears his father's voice, telling him to fight on. It is enough. It will always be enough.

title: The Ancestral Voice
nickname: Mundhum Devi, She Who Sings the Songs of Creation
lore: In the same Limbuwan region where Yangtangza wields the ancestral axe, there lived a family of shamans who were the keepers of the Mundhum—the sacred oral scriptures of the Limbu people. These scriptures contained not just history, but the very songs of creation, the words that had shaped the world. Ishaah was born into this family on the day of the annual Udhauli festival, when the Limbu people celebrate the descent of the ancestors to earth. Her grandmother, a powerful shamaness named Namsem, saw the omens: the ancestors had chosen this child to be their voice. From age five, Ishaah was trained in the Mundhum. She learned the songs of creation, the stories of the ancestors, the chants that could heal and protect. By ten, she could recite the entire creation epic from memory. By fourteen, she could chant in the language of the spirits, and they would answer. When Ishaah was eighteen, a plague swept through the Limbu villages. It was no ordinary sickness—it was a spiritual disease, caused by a dark sorcerer who had poisoned the ancestral spirits. Her grandmother, weakened by age, could not fight it alone. She performed a final ritual, transferring the full power of the Mundhum to Ishaah, and then passed into the spirit world. Ishaah, now the sole keeper of the sacred songs, walked through the villages, chanting the healing verses, purifying the spirits, driving out the plague. She saved hundreds, but the effort left her changed—she could now see and speak with the ancestors at will, and they guided her every word. Now, at twenty-seven, Ishaah is known across Limbuwan as the Ancestral Voice. She performs the great rituals, sings the songs of creation, and guides her people through times of trouble. She is a quiet, gentle woman, her curves as soft as her songs, her eyes holding the wisdom of generations. She is Ishaah Limbu, and the ancestors speak through her.
description: Ishaah Limbu is a vision of ancestral beauty and sacred grace—a woman whose curves are as soft as her songs, whose presence is as ancient as the mountains, whose eyes hold the wisdom of generations. She stands at five feet two inches, her body a masterpiece of feminine curves and spiritual grace. Her figure is the idealized shamaness's silhouette: a narrow waist that seems almost impossibly small, accentuated by the tight-fitting cholo she wears; hips that flare generously, curved and full, swaying with the rhythm of ancient chants; thighs soft yet strong, supporting her as she sits for hours in meditation; and a bosom full and magnificent, straining against the fabric of her cholo, the upper curves tastefully visible, a symbol of her nurturing nature. Her skin is the color of warm honey with golden undertones, smooth and luminous, almost glowing in the light of ritual fires. Her face is a study in classical Limbu beauty—a perfect oval with high, gentle cheekbones that catch light softly, a straight delicate nose, and full lips the color of rose petals, always curved in a gentle, mysterious smile. But her eyes are her most captivating feature: they are large, almond-shaped, and the color of deep, warm brown with flecks of gold that shimmer when she chants. They hold the wisdom of generations, the peace of the ancestors, and the infinite compassion of one who sings for all souls. Her hair is a magnificent cascade of jet-black silk, so long it falls past her waist, thick and lustrous, with natural waves. She wears it loose, flowing around her like a dark river, often adorned with small bells and feathers from sacred birds. On her forehead, she wears a silver tikka shaped like a sun, with a small ruby at its center. Her attire is traditional Limbu shaman clothing, rich with symbolism. She wears a cholo of deep red silk, fitted perfectly to her form, the neckline cut low enough to reveal the upper curves of her full bosom. The cholo is embroidered with gold thread in patterns of ancestors, spirits, and sacred symbols. Over the cholo, she wears a shorter jacket of black silk, open at the front, with more ancestral patterns. Around her neck, she wears multiple strands: a necklace of dzi beads, each one ancient and powerful; a chain with a pendant shaped like a Mundhum scroll; and a leather cord holding a small pouch of sacred herbs. On her wrists, she wears delicate silver bangles that chime when she chants. On her fingers, she wears several silver rings with turquoise and coral. Around her waist, she wears a wide silver belt from which hang small bells that ring with her movements, adding rhythm to her chants. On her legs, she wears a long skirt of deep red, reaching her ankles, with gold embroidery of ancestors and spirits. Underneath, she wears warm leggings. On her feet, she wears soft leather sandals, often barefoot in sacred spaces. When she chants, a soft golden light emanates from her, and those nearby feel the presence of ancestors—warm, protective, loving. She is Ishaah Limbu, the Ancestral Voice, and the spirits sing through her.

story.part1: Ishaah was born in a Limbu village in the eastern hills on the day of the Udhauli festival, when ancestors descend to earth. Her grandmother, Namsem, a powerful shamaness, saw the ancestors bless the child and knew she was special. She named her Ishaah—'Divine Song'—hoping she would sing for all people.
story.part2: Her childhood was spent learning the Mundhum. By age five, she could recite simple verses. By ten, she knew the entire creation epic. Her grandmother taught her that the songs were not just words—they were power, they were life, they were the ancestors' gift.
story.part3: At fourteen, she could chant in the language of the spirits, and they would answer. The villagers began to see her as a shaman, though she was still young. Her grandmother was proud, but also worried—such power came with great responsibility.
story.part4: When Ishaah was eighteen, a plague swept through the villages—a spiritual disease caused by a dark sorcerer. Her grandmother, weakened by age, could not fight it alone. She transferred the full power of the Mundhum to Ishaah and passed into the spirit world.
story.part5: Ishaah walked through the villages, chanting the healing verses for days without rest. She purified the spirits, drove out the plague, saved hundreds. But the effort left her changed—she could now see and speak with ancestors at will.
story.part6: For the next nine years, she became the spiritual guide of her people. She performed rituals, sang the creation songs, and communed with the ancestors. Her reputation grew, and she became known as the Ancestral Voice.
story.part7: She has guided her people through droughts, floods, wars, and plagues. The ancestors speak through her, warning of danger, offering wisdom, blessing crops and marriages.
story.part8: She has found a kindred spirit in Yangtangza, the Yalambar's Heir. He fights for the people; she prays for them. Together, they are the strength of the Limbu nation—the axe and the song.
story.part9: She knows that the dark sorcerer who caused the plague may return. When he does, she will be ready. The ancestors will protect her, and her songs will drive him back.
story.part10: Now, at twenty-seven, Ishaah continues her sacred work. She sings for the living and the dead, for the past and the future, for all who need her voice. She is Ishaah Limbu, and the ancestors will never be silent.

ultimate_skill.description: Ishaah's gold-flecked eyes blaze with light, and she opens the Mundhum scroll. She begins to chant the Song of Creation—the original verses that shaped the universe. The words become visible, golden and glowing, floating in the air around her. Reality itself responds: enemies are held in place by the power of the song, allies are healed and strengthened, and the very landscape reshapes according to the chant. When the song ends, the scroll closes, and Ishaah stands at the center, her chest heaving, her eyes slowly dimming. She has sung the song of creation. She has reminded the world of its origins. She is Ishaah Limbu, the Ancestral Voice, and the ancestors will never be silent.
